utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the context in which the response should be assessed is that of the clear standard for the admission of an accused's statement against a co-accused. The Appeals Chamber has made clear that such statements should only be excluded in exceptional circumstances that would render the statement devoid of probative value. And this is clear from the Prlic and Popovic Appeals Chamber decisions that are cited in our motion There's nothing raised in the response that would point to any such exceptional circumstances, either individually or cumulatively. First, the allegations that General Cermak was somehow improperly coached into providing certain answers is based on a microscopic examination of particular extracts of an interview that had been taken out of context and then mis-characterized as coaching. Secondly, the claim that certain statements made by General Cermak are uncorroborated, even if it were true, is not a basis for their exclusion, but, in fact, they're not true. These claims are similarly based on mis-characterizations of General Cermak's words and of the evidence. First I would like to address the allegations that General Cermak was coached during his 2004 interview. These allegations, Your Honours, have to be assessed in light of the overall context of this interview. And, Your Honours, when you read the transcript of this interview, and watch the video of this interview, it is clear that Cermak is unequivocally and at times adamantly asserting the same position he has asserted all along since 1998. There are few interventions by his counsel; but in any event, Cermak is clearly in control and he pays little attention to these relatively few and minor interjections. Secondly, General Cermak was entitled to consult with his counsel, and his counsel was entitled to consult with and advise General Cermak during the interview. The mere existence of a few interjections by counsel is not in and of itself inappropriate. And in the response, these brief verbal exchanges are taken out of context, and mis-characterized as counsel, quote, coaching General Cermak to provide certain statements about General Gotovina to OTP investigators. Your Honours when these exchanges are placed back there their context, these are marked; one, don't show that General Cermak was coached into providing statements by General Gotovina; and two, in any event, are insufficient to render the interview unreliable or inadmissible. When these statements are viewed in their context, General Cermak's counsel is either advising General Cermak to answer the question that he was asked; advising General Cermak to clarify the manner in which the question was asked or the way the answer is given; or simple repeating a position that General Cermak had already made clear sometimes on several occasions. And I would like to go through a couple of examples. And the first one is in -- is the first one raised in the response, and this is at page 17 of Annex A of the response. And this is the interjection by Mr. Prodanovic where he says: "Communication with Gotovina, communication with Gotovina, yes." And General Cermak says, "Yes, fine." And Mr. Prodanovic says: "Say, it, say it." And a few lines later he says: "When you see each our how do you get along, do you get along?" And General Cermak says: "Uh-huh, that previous question. And Ms. Slokovic says: "Are you every day, Mr. Prodanovic, are you every day? And General Cermak, "Oh no that is ..." Your Honours, the key to understanding this interjection is General Cermak's statement, "Uh-huh that previous question." And, in fact, if you go back to page 7 of this same interview, this is where the context of this interjection begins. And at page 7, the investigator asks: "Okay. Can I first ask you about your relationship with General Gotovina and how it actually worked together when you -- your time in Knin?" Then own the next page, the investigator again: "We're good. Okay, so how did it really work? How was, how were your tasks separated, how did you communicate? Perhaps" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, would you kindly slow down for the sake of the interpretations, especially when you're reading. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I apologise. The investigator says: "How did you communicate? Perhaps you could explain on a day-to-day basis how it actually operated." Cermak then begins to speak and for two pages, does not answer that question. At page 10, the investigator asks again: "Okay. We'll come back to your tasking by the president. I'll go back to my question at the beginning, your relationship, your day-to-day relationship with General Gotovina from day one." On the next page the investigator asks again: "Okay. And then what happened? Presumably would you have been given an office. And Gotovina would have had an office. Was there any plan to communicate on a daily basis? How was it set up?" Cermak continues and he again doesn't answer this question. Then on pages 13 and 14. There's an intervention by Mr. Prodanovic that is not included in the response. First he complains that the translation of the question was not quite correct, that the question was about General Cermak's relationship with Gotovina on a day-to-day basis and how they communicated, and notes that General Cermak has not yet answered that question. Then Mr. Prodanovic reminds General Cermak that that question was about communication with Gotovina, and advised General Cermak to answer that question. For two more page, Cermak again fails to answer that question. It is it then, Your Honours, that we reach the page that is included in the response and that is the context in which Mr. Prodanovic says: "Communication with Gotovina, communication with Gotovina, say it, say it." And then, finally, at page 21, the investigator runs once more to his original question. He says: "Okay. So I'll still go back to my original question. How did you operate with Gotovina when he was actually in Knin? Did you meet on a daily basis? Did you -- how did this contact work?" And then, Your Honours, General Cermak answers the question and he answers it without interruption. Your Honours, this example cited in the response is not coaching. It is it General Cermak's counsel advising General Cermak quite appropriately to answer the question he was asked. He is not suggesting any answer to him, and he is certainly not telling General Cermak to provide certain statements about Gotovina to OTP investigators as the response claims. A second example, is the one cited at pages 30 to 31 of the response, in the Annex to the response. And this an assertion, this is the foundation for the assertion at paragraph 9 of the response that General Cermak was coached to state that General Gotovina, "Was informed of crimes by members of the international community." Well, first of all, what General Cermak actually said in this passage was that, "Everything that was written to me by the international community, he," meaning General Gotovina, "was also informed about that." General Cermak was not even stating that General Gotovina was informed of crimes by members of the international community. So it is hard to imagine how this could have been coached. In any event, it's difficult to see how General Cermak's answer, actual answer could have been coached by Mr. Prodanovic's advice to General Cermak, quote, to mention international organisations. This is -- if you look at the video of approximately two-second intervention by Mr. Prodanovic and it is not suggestive of any particular answer. General Cermak then says, Everything that was written to me by international community, he was also informed about that. And again in context, General Cermak has just finished a laundry list of sources of information that General Gotovina had on the previous brief page. He says, I just explained what his possibilities were of getting information. All three services. He had his commander, units of on the ground. His commanders also had to reacts and had to punish. He had the SIS. He had the military police. It is then that there is the intervention by Mr. Prodanovic and General Cermak's statement everything that was written to me by the international community he was also informed about that. This is simply a logical conclusion of what General Cermak has said on the previous page. A third example, page 34, of the annex to the response. And this is a claim that General Cermak was coached into making a statement that, "there was no handover between me and Gotovina." If you actually look at what Mr. Prodanovic said, Mr. Prodanovic advised Mr. Cermak to, "get him to show you the handover." This is simply advice to Mr. Cermak to be shown any relevant document about a matter under discussion. This is it a classically appropriate intervention by counsel that in no way could be considered to be coaching. But in any event General Cermak ignored the advice. He didn't ask for a document he just stated: "There was no handover between me and Gotovina." This was just a repetition of what Cermak had state add few lines earlier when he said the claim that was a such a hand over was "nonsense." And finally, the example contained at page 36 and the annex to the response, and this is a claim that General Cermak was coached into stating that on the 6th of August, video meeting, General Gotovina was not upset about crimes but that Knin was dirty and that President Tudjman was coming to town. And that's at paragraph 9 of the response. Well, firstly, General Cermak's statement at page 36 that General Gotovina was upset about the "mess in Knin" reflects comments that are made in that video itself which is in evidence, and which Cermak had stated that he had just watched. Secondly, General Cermak stated that: "General Gotovina was upset not about the situation but because the president was coming to town and bus his darling Susak was arriving." This was a statement General Cermak said before there was any intervention by his counsel. It was only then that Mr. Prodanovic said -- stated he wasn't upset about crimes. In essence, Mr. Prodanovic is just repeating what General Cermak has already said, moreover, Mr. Prodanovic was reiterating a statement General Cermak had made just a few pages earlier when he was asked, at page 34, what General Gotovina's reaction was when Cermak raised the issues of crimes with him. General Cermak said: "His reaction was yes, we know, we'll handle that. I was far more upset than he was." But, again, Your Honour, General Cermak ignored the comment made by his counsel. He did not repeat, Mr. Prodanovic's remark that General Cermak was not upset about crimes. What he said was: "He wasn't upset about what the military had done but because the town was dirty and there were no state signs anywhere, and that's very clear on that tape." This is not a coached statement. This is it clearly General Cermak commenting on what he has seen on the tape and stating his own position on what happened at that meeting. Your Honour, the other examples cited in the response are all similar in nature. In anticipation of written submissions, we have prepared a chart setting out the context of each of these statements, and explaining that what I've just stated that these remarks don't amount to coaching, and I would be happy to go through each of those now. I'd also be happy to distribute that chart to the parties and the Bench. I don't know what the Court prefers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have you given a copy to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because it is a by the difficult if it is the last opportunity to respond to that. At the same time, I take it that the chart you have done it in a concise way, so one option would be to give it now to the Defence, so that at least they can have a look at it; and either invite you to say aloud what -- it is clear to us -- the problem is that if the Defence hasn't heard your interpretation of the matters it is very difficult for them to -- if they would wish to resupply, but I could not exclude that they are not aware of what you said. So that is a basic principle of fairness in the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour I wasn't aware that the team had granted the request to certify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, if you say -- well, it always depends on what you submit, isn't it? I just said I could not exclude for the possibility that they wish to -- and that's maybe an understatement.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour I just -- this would have been attached to the written --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's move. On how much time would it take you to just to briefly point at -- you say it is all similar. Perhaps in short even if you would summarise your argument where it has been given a bit more detail then at least the Defence has had notice.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. The example at page 29 of the appendix to the response. This was reminder by counsel to General Cermak to answer a question that had been asked in a hypothetical manner in a hypothetical fashion and the full context of this exchange can be found at pages 22 to 32 of the interview. The next one is pages 30 to 31 of the annex. Again, the full context of this exchange is at pages 22 to 32.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly switch off all unnecessary microphones. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: The example at pages 32 to 33 of the annex. This was simply an intervention by counsel asking General Cermak to clarify his answer, by clarifying who this group of people were associated with. There is no suggestion of any answer. At page 35 in the annex, the full context of this exchange at a pages 32 to 43 of the interview. Mr. Prodanovic was simply repeating a position that Cermak had taken earlier, about his -- about his role as an administrative general. At page 43 of the annex, Mr. Prodanovic interrupts General Cermak before he makes an answer by saying, No, no. Full context of this exchange is at pages 32 to 46 of the interview. And the intervention was simply a reiteration of the position that General Cermak had just stated. At pages 44 to 45 of the annex, General Cermak had just stated that he had nothing to do with the military forces in the area, and then Mr. Prodanovic interrupts General Cermak by saying, You never commanded, which was again just repeating what he said immediately prior. And the full context of this exchange is at pages 43 to 45 of the interview. At page 46 of the annex, again, Mr. Prodanovic interrupts General Cermak by saying, But you were not there in response to the planning of the military operation. Full context is at pages 45 and 46, and this is merely a repetition of what Mr. Cermak had said earlier about not being involved in the planning of Operation Storm. At page 52, of the annex, firstly this has nothing to do with General Gotovina. But again the intervention is simply Mr. Prodanovic stating, "international community," and General Cermak continuing his answer. And it is consistent with statements Mr. Cermak had made previously. At page 60 of the annex, Mr. Prodanovic is simply advising Mr. Cermak to clarify the way he is giving his answer, by stating it would be somewhere in writing, after Mr. Cermak denied being in charge. At page 64 of the annex, Mr. Prodanovic interrupted General Cermak by stating: "You did not command them or the military police." Firstly the full context of this exchange is at pages 62 through 65, and this statement is consistent with Mr. Cermak's position that he had made clear in many previous occasions during this interview and previous interviews. Similarly at page 96 of the response, the interruption by Mr. Prodanovic was to state: "It not your job to inform them." Which was again a repetition of something Mr. Cermak had said on many previous occasions that he no authority over the police. At page 102 in the annex, Mr. Prodanovic simply said: "And the coordinator." And if you look the full context of this exchange is at pages 97 to 103. And finally at pages 163 to 164, in the annex, Mr. Prodanovic asked Cermak to explain that had Mr. Cermak been under the Main Staff then he could receive and then Mr. Cermak interrupts Mr. Prodanovic and says, I have said all of this already, and tells him to calm down and then Mr. Cermak explains that he has said this all before; but if this had been the command structure then he would have received his orders from General Gotovina and the Main Staff. Your Honours, when these interventions are looked at in the context of the interview as a whole and throughout three interviews there are relatively view of them. They're short. They're largely innocuous and not suggestive of anything. To the extent they may be seen as suggesting some kind of an answer, they are generally ignored or given short shrift by General Cermak, who is quite focussed on telling his own story. Your Honours, we have prepared a version of the 2004 interview with all of these interruptions by counsel translated. They have not been translated before because it was just a transcription, and we would be happy to provide that to the Chamber and replace the version that we had tendered earlier, with this revised version. And now I'd just lying to briefly cover the second aspect of the response, which is the alleged lack of corroboration of certain -- of General Cermak's remarks that relate to General Gotovina. The claim is that these remarks are uncorroborated and therefore unreliable. Well, even if this claim were true, this would not make any of these statements, quote, patently unreliable or otherwise amount to a proper basis for their exclusion. And that is clear from the Appeals Chamber jurisprudence on this issue. But, in fact, the claim is not accurate. The claim is premised on mis-characterizations of Mr. Cermak's actual words and the state of the evidence. For example, at paragraph 20 of the response it is claimed that General Cermak stated that Forand and other internationals met with General Gotovina "to discuss the commission of crimes," and then claims that this statement lacks corroboration. Well, first, that is a mis-characterization of General Cermak's words. General Cermak was asked if he ever referred internationals who reported or complained about crimes to General Gotovina and Cermak stated that internationals including Forand: "Did go and talk to General Gotovina. They didn't only talk to me. General Forand went to see General Gotovina several times. Other people went to see him." This is at page 51 of the 2001 interview. General Cermak doesn't say anything about the purpose of these meetings. And his actual words are quite specifically corroborated by the evidence of General Forand, who described two meetings that he held with General Gotovina and described complaining about the commission of crimes at both of those meetings. But in any event, there is actually evidence that members of the international community met with General Gotovina for the express purpose of discussing crimes. So even the version as it is mis-characterized is corroborated. This is supported by a statement that has been tendered by the Defence, of Witness 174; and that is Exhibit D898, Witness 174 stated in relation to his meeting with General Gotovina that: "The crimes committed in Sector South were one of the two subjects I wanted to raise during the meeting."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The submission by the Prosecution misses the forest for the trees, Mr. President. And, as a matter of fact, in the submission we see exactly what the fundamental point is here, which is the Prosecution and the Defence can now engage in an argument about what is or isn't corroborated in the statement. The reason we have to engage in that argument, of course, is because General Gotovina's fundamental right to cross-examine witnesses under Article 21, is impeded by this procedure. And many of the questions, both from the Prosecution and the Defence, about what is or isn't corroborated would, of course, would be normally in the normal course put to a witness, challenged, tested, and the Chamber can then come to own conclusions about what a particular witness in a statement said or didn't say, meant or didn't mean, and what is or isn't corroborated. That is the fundamental issue here, and the fact that we've gone through there exercise now for 20 minutes to half an hour trying to pick through what is or isn't corroborated, what is or isn't coaching actually goes to the fundamental point, which is, again, this can't be tested. Now, with respect to the point about coaching, I submit to you, Your Honour, that what you see on that video is a law school example of coaching. The reason is, and I would put it to the Prosecution, how would the Prosecution feel about, for example, letting a lawyer now in the courtroom sit next to witnesses and be able to whisper answers to witness who is are testifying before the Chamber. I have a sneaky suspicion that the Prosecution probably wouldn't like that procedure. Now, why is it coaching? An attorney in representing a client at a deposition or at a suspect interview, particularly at suspect interview is present because of the rights that a suspect has under the Rules of Procedure, means Rules 42 through 44, and in particular the right to remain silent and to not incriminate himself with statements made during that interview. That is a role of an attorney at a suspect interview. It is the job of an attorney at a suspect interview to make legal objections to questions that are being posed, or to provide legal advice; for example, Do not answer that question because it may tend to incriminate you. We have gone through this, and I believe based on what I heard, that the Prosecution will concede that many, if not all of these interventions, involve advice as to how to testify on the facts, which is per se, coaching. Because it is not allowed under the Rules. The lawyers were there to make legal objections, not to make factual clarifications, assertions, et cetera. It is per se coaching. Now, the way that the Prosecution is reading the words actually asks you to ignore the reality of the situation which is that these suspect interviews involved preparation, which I believe the Prosecution will concede. Preparation between counsel and the accused as to what potential questions may come up during the suspect interview, what the answers are to the questions that will be posed. So a subset of coaching is, of course, queueing, which is what has already been rehearsed in the preparation for the suspect interview is then queued by using certain words or phrases in order to remind the deponent of what has been discussed prior to coming to the suspect interview. Again, these are issues that we can argue back and forth. These are issues that would be developed in cross-examination, which cannot obviously take place here as these statements come in. The context of these interviews is something that we would gladly explore if given the opportunity. The context of the 2004 interview is that the statements are given in the detention unit; the statements are given after the Trial Chamber denied provisional release; and the statements are given after the Prosecutor asserted that if the accused would give a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor, in exchange, the Prosecution will not oppose a renewed provisional release motion. That's the context of this, and I would be happy to debate this context further. I believe it is relevant. Again, these are all issues that would be addressed in cross-examination. Now, Prosecution says that we are addressing particular microscopic aspects of the -- of the interview. It just so happens that that the microscopic aspects of it are the ones that deal with General Gotovina, which is obviously all that we're concerned about. So to that extent, whether you wish to classify it as microscopic or not, our interest in this is only as it relates to the use of the statement as against our client. Furthermore, the standard to be applied is not the standard that has been discussed by the Prosecution. The standard is as it states in Rule 89 (D). Rule 89 (D) obviously says if the need to ensure a fair trial outweighs the probative value, then it can be excluded by the Chamber. That is the standard to apply. We submit that in light of the fact that there is no cross-examination that can take place here, and in light of the fact that there is a clear coaching as legally understood, clear queueing, then that has to be a factor to be considered under Rule 89 (D); furthermore as is relates to corroboration, the Prosecution does not actually -- and I would add that the Prlic decision one of the factors explicitly mentioned by the Appeals Chamber that have to be considered as to admissibility is corroboration or the use of the statement, includes corroboration of the statements made. Now, I go back to some of the cited portions and some of the coaching and it says, for example, at page 36, the coaching is: "He wasn't upset because of crimes." Then there's a next question, which is not transcribed from General Cermak to his lawyer: "He wasn't what?" Again the lawyer says: "Upset because of crimes." Then the answer that comes out at the end is: "He wasn't upset about what the military had done but because the town was all dirty and there were no state signs anywhere." Now, if the Prosecution is going to stipulate that that statement made, "he wasn't upset about what the military had done," doesn't relate to crimes, we have no problem. If that's the -- if we can get that stipulation from the Prosecution. On the other hand, if it is going to be used by the Prosecution to say in closing argument General Cermak said -- doesn't -- that he wasn't upset about crime, and that's how you should interpret the sentence, then obviously it is coaching, and it can be not be tested on cross-examination. We cannot see if that would still be the position of the declarant today. I would add that the Prosecution has not gone through, and quite frankly, is in the position of vouching now for one of the accused but won't actually come out and say which portions they're vouching for, as the Prosecution and I will take a look if there's a submission; in light of the Prlic Appeals Chamber's decision, if the Prosecution is willing to state these claims, we believe, are corroborated, these are not; then we need to know what the Prosecution itself believes about whether these are corroborated. For example, again, I go back to the statement. Perhaps there's a misinterpretation by either the Prosecution or the Defence about the statement at page 30, which was -- and the top of page 31 which says: "Everything that was written to me by the international community he was also informed about that." Now, does that mean that the international community also informed him about that, or does that mean that the substance of the matters was given to him, even though not by the international community? If it is the former, and if that's the position of the Prosecution, then, again, we go and look to see whether the Prosecution believes that statement is corroborated; and we again call your attention to the fact that the Prosecution's own declared expert Mr. Theunens was examined on this point and himself stated that he could find no evidence, no written evidence of any such notice from the international community representatives to General Gotovina. Again, that gets us involved in a situation of how do we interpret this, what does this mean, et cetera? If the Prosecution will stipulate that that sentence doesn't mean that General Gotovina was advised by the international community, we have no issue; but the problem results from the issue that we have no ability to cross-examine. I will wrap up again, Mr. President, and Your Honours by saying in this particular situation according to the Appeals Chamber jurisprudence and according to Rule 89 (D), the Trial Chamber has the discretion to admit or exclude this evidence. We submit -- as it relates to General Gotovina. We submit, Your Honours, that the factors to consider are, in fact, the coaching which take -- took place here, which was improper; the overall circumstances and lack of corroboration, at least as it relates to General Gotovina and assertions and interrogations of those words, that could be put forward by the Prosecution; we submit that the tendering of these documents at this stage of the proceedings is also something that you should consider, because unlike the Prlic case, which is still ongoing, but the statements tendered in the midst of the Prosecution's case in chief, the Prosecution tenders these at the end of the case, where anything that could have been in dispute by the parties about how to interpret these words could have been addressed with -- through witnesses or otherwise addressed. We submit, Your Honours, that the appropriate remedy, which would ensure the admission of the statements vis-a-vis the declarants of the statements but also protect the fundamental rights of General Gotovina under Article 21 is to redact those portions of the statement as they relate to General Gotovina or otherwise that the statements can not be used against General Gotovina in order to -- under Rule 89 (D) in order to protect his fundamental rights under Article 21 of the Statute. Thank you very much.

utterances.text: Thank you. There is an issue about a -- four documents not being tendered at a time when Witness 43 testified. I do understand that they are now submitted as bar table documents, although dealt with, I think, and intended to be used with Witness 43.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Your Honour, Witness 43 was submitted through a Rule 92 quater, so he didn't testify; but there was an issue -- initially it was 92 bis filing and the Chamber invited the Defence to state the basis for their objection to the admission of the statement where they attached some of the statements to their response. The Prosecution later found out that Witness 43 is now unavailable to testify and refiled under 92 quater.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the witness where a 92 bis motion was denied and then he was then --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: We have found out that he had passed away in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and the Defence opposed admission of the 92 quater decision. Could I hear the position of the Defence on these four documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe the first as a -- for the record I believe that the witness had actually passed away before the 92 bis application was filed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That could be the case. At least we were not aware. I think also the Prosecution may not have been aware of the witness having passed away before it filed the 92 bis submission.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Again, Mr. President, just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I think, Mr. President, the issue was that it was Defence documents not Prosecution documents, I think, that were at issue for Witness 43 and that Prosecution's position was if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just try to ... . Yes, it was Gotovina Defence bar table submission for witness 43 to which the Prosecution should still respond. I apologise for going in the wrong direction. Let me just -- the bar table submission is ... let me just have a look. It newly came up. I see, as a matter of fact, that the bar table submission concerns -- I think concerned six documents, but two of them were already in evidence. That is the special report from the Croatian Ministry of Defence, which is Exhibit D178; (redacted) (redacted) that was -- I'm afraid that ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, your microphone is on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have a list of six: D178 is already in evidence; P1397 is already in evidence; what then remains is 1D00-0847; next one, 1D00-0869; 1D00-0872; and 1D00-0882. I think I'm now working on the wrong -- the proper direction again, Mr. Misetic. Is there any objection against -- yes, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I just wish to be clear here, as I understand the procedural state - and I could be wrong - there is an pending Rule 92 quater motion. There has been a response by us opposing. Last housekeeping session, Mr. President, you invited me if we wished to bar table something, so it should be qualified that our bar table is contingent upon your ruling on whether the statement is coming in through Rule 92 quater.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And similarly any statement of new objection of the Prosecution for these documents would be contingent on the statement being admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that is clear, but then there would be no objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is on the record. So if the 92 quater statement will be admitted into evidence, and I think the parties will know that by tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: There was one issue, and I'm going from memory here so I apologise if I'm mistaken. Some of the documents because they were only for the purpose of the opposition had only been partially translated some witness statements so -- if they are into evidence we would obviously we would like to have the full translation because it would be part of evidence now not just in opposition. But that's just from my memory. But if they are into evidence we obviously want full translations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That was one document where consisting of four pages where two were translated, only pages one and four. Thank you. That's on the record, so the Chamber is in the position to decide all the issues here. Then we have ten minutes left only, and I would like to start already with the MFI list, so as to see if we can make any progress in this respect. We'll then --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's an also housekeeping issue. Since it is not on the MFI list, I don't know if it is something that we can deal with first but we have e complete list. That's the Rajcic bar table motion. There are no numbers assigned to that. We can do that tomorrow as well, but since there were no numbers assigned perhaps it would be prudent to do that first. But I leave it to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It appears on -- all of the them do appear on my MFI list. I don't know whether, on the latest version, the ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was just informed that it came in, in morning and sometimes and in court I'm not able to look what comes in. They will be provisionally assigned exhibit numbers. I've got no idea what it is at this moment, but then at least they're on our list to further be looked into tomorrow. I would not be surprised if the Defence would jump up and say it's rather late. Although I do understand that it was rather early. We'll have that. The registrar is asked to assign provisional numbers to those documents and then we will, unless there is any other matter we should deal with before continuing with the MFI list. The first one appearing is D568. We have extensively dealt with that. The next one, Mr. Mikulicic, D1083. If there's still no translation --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, unfortunately, there is it still no translation. Mr. Waespi and have I been exchanged a rather amount of communication. I just can remind the Chamber that we started with this issue on 28th of November last year, so it has been a long time passed on. But I believe we are going to have a translation very soon. But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would need the Chamber's assistance and the Chamber appreciated the hard work and the difficulties CLSS may have in giving priority to one or another document, at the same time we're now at a point where the Prosecution's case is close to being concluded. So, therefore, the Chamber would offer its assistance. But, again, not as a form of criticism but as a way of smoothing the path to -- to conclusions of the Prosecution's case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes. I -- I think I could say on behalf of Mr. Waespi we are grateful, Your Honour, and we will ask for your assistance, if that would be need in the near future. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then we move on. I will read tomorrow a brief decision on D1212. I then come to D1302. This is a table created by the Cermak Defence, analysing Annex 1 of the CHC report. I think the issue -- there were two issues. The first one was the verification of the content. Has this been done, Mr. Russo?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. President, with respect to D1302, all the way through D1305, we have no objection to those on the previously stated bases now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the problems with the titles have been resolved as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: That's correct Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1302, up to and including D1305, are admitted into evidence. Then we are at D1307, statement of Petar Pasic. Prosecution has taken the position that it should only admit it as to those portions on which the witness gave some evidence and not the statement in its entirety. Now, I'd like to further hear from the parties whether there have been further exchanges, whether there's any agreement on the matter, or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. President, our position remains the same, with respect to that exhibit, that, as to those portions not discussed, that the statement has to remain marked for identification until the witness comes and fulfils the requirements of 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: We can accept that position, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which would mean that, if the Cermak Defence seeks this to be in evidence, that they'll first wait whether there's a Defence case at all; and if there is an Defence case, that then they would call the witness. Is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour. I think that is the best way of putting it, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, D1307 is vacated that's at least, Mr. Cayley, it can be vacated. It is not tendered anymore into evidence. Then we come to D1331. That is the letter sent by the public prosecutor's office to the law firm of Mikulicic. Mr. Mikulicic, I think the only thing is the decision of the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Admission of D1331 is denied. It's not admitted. The next one is D1429. There may be -- there are two issues here first. First, is that no dock ID number was assigned at the time that this document was tendered. That's the first issue. And the second issue might that be the transcript reads that the Prosecution objected, objection. But since it usually explained why and here it is not, there is an reason to believe that the intention was to say no objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: That's correct Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Has a dock ID been assigned Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It has been uploaded?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It has.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then D1429 is admitted into evidence. D1434. What was still needed is that the Chamber would decide on mission. The Chamber denies admission into evidence of D1434. Therefore, it gets the status of non-admitted. D1439 has been litigated and is waiting for a decision by the Chamber. D1439 is admitted into evidence. We now come to a long list of prints. I think it would be unwise to start with it at 16 minutes before 2.00. Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Regarding D1439, the Chamber, on the record had stated that at that time there had been no sufficient basis presented for the admission, so I'm just wondering if we'll get reasons on what had changed during that statement by the Chamber on the record and today's decision, just so that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll check the record and provide you with short reasons as soon as possible, most likely tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Could I inquire because of my own personal schedule how long do we intend to sit all day tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Much depends on --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: On us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The MFI list will take us -- MFI list will take us perhaps another hour, that's -- then I have to read a few short decisions, admission into evidence, which will take perhaps some 10 to 15 minutes. We have six of them, more lengthy decisions, that will take another half an hour. I think that approximately two and a half hours all together would be needed tomorrow. That's my first assessment. But, at the same time, on some matters we have even received the submissions so, therefore, it is very difficult to assess whether that would create a need for any further questions to the parties. For example, I do not know to what extent the Appendixes B and C to the response to 568 will create additional -- additional problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I just wish to remind the Court, as I advised you last week, I'm supposed to be in a different proceeding tomorrow, but I will see what I can do with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you please try to -- it is not for that reason that we said that as you are aware of now that we didn't ask for the Prosecution to prepare for witnesses. But -- tried to the extent possible to pass this on to your learned colleagues, and I know it is not easy sometimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It's a judge, and if I could get a note from my judge; so I can pass to the other judge. I'm just kidding. So, yes, I will try to pass that on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, the problem is, of course, we would have time on Thursday and Friday as well, but we are at a point where we would like to have the Prosecution's case concluded, so that we can proceed and that's the only reason why it is a bit difficult to accommodate you. If you have any priority. If you say tomorrow this or this issue, I'd like it deal with first and let's leave all the other stuff to -- to one of your colleagues that, of course, we would consider that. But then please inform us as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Very briefly, Your Honour just so that we can advance things quickly tomorrow; for the next three exhibits, the Prosecution Exhibits. That's P01050, P01051, and P01057; that was the subject of oral submissions, which Your Honours will find at transcript reference 11444. No decision was made but you may well be aware of that already, but your staff might be able to give you that, and we with move quickly through those tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for this observation. We will adjourn for the day, but not until after I have expressed my admiration for transcribing so many numbers, and it's not the first time, and so accurate. We will resume tomorrow, Wednesday, 4th of March, 9.00, Courtroom I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 4th day of March, 2009, at 9.00 a.m.
